claims.evidence: This is supported by phrenic nerve recordings under different pH conditions shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: In Spi1−/− preparations at E18.5, lowering the pH from 7.4 to 7.2 induces a significant increase in phrenic burst frequency from 10.1 ± 0.3 to 16.9±0.9 bursts/min.
claims.source: Similarly, however, in mutant littermates (n = 5), an equivalent aCSF acidification also induced a significant increase in phrenic burst frequency from 10.1 ± 0.3 to 16.9±0.9 bursts/min (p < 0.001, Figure 6C, right).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phrenic nerve recordings under different pH conditions shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The final respiratory drive to phrenic motoneurons continues to express centrally detected pH changes in the Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5.
claims.source: This finding therefore demonstrated that despite a reduced frequency and a diminished epF network, the final respiratory drive to phrenic motoneurons continues to express centrally detected pH changes in the Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5, further confirming that the central chemosensitive property of the epf network is preserved.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the pH responsiveness data from phrenic nerve recordings.

claims.claim: The central chemosensitive property of the epF network is preserved in Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5.
claims.source: This finding therefore demonstrated that despite a reduced frequency and a diminished epF network, the final respiratory drive to phrenic motoneurons continues to express centrally detected pH changes in the Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5, further confirming that the central chemosensitive property of the epf network is preserved.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the pH responsiveness data.

claims.claim: Bursts of activity in one C4 root are strictly coordinated with those of the contralateral root in Spi1−/− mutants at E18.5, with a mean delay of 0.8 ± 4 ms.
claims.source: Indeed, bursts of activity in one C4 root were strictly coordinated with those of the contralateral root, with a mean delay of 0.8 ± 4 ms in the Spi1−/− mutant (range from −51.8 to 142.4 ms; n = 5, 14 bursts per preparation), similar (p = 0.6) to that observed in WT preparations (mean: 2.07 ± 4.6 ms; range from −77.6 to 149.1 ms; n = 5, 15 bursts per preparation).
claims.evidence: This is supported by bilateral phrenic nerve recordings shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The bilateral synchronization of the central respiratory command to the two phrenic motor pools is unaffected by the absence of microglia in the Spi1−/− mutant at E18.5.
claims.source: Thus, the bilateral synchronization of the central respiratory command to the two phrenic motor pools that derives from the epF and preBötC networks acting in combination is apparently unaffected by the absence of microglia in the Spi1−/− mutant at the late prenatal stage.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the bilateral phrenic nerve recordings showing synchrony.

claims.claim: 14 out of 15 WT embryos at E18.5 expressed sustained rhythmic breathing movements at a mean frequency of 102.4 ± 3 breaths/min.
claims.source: Of the WT embryos, 14/15 animals expressed sustained rhythmic breathing movements in response to mechanical stimulation at a mean frequency of 102.4 ± 3 breaths/min (Figure 7A), whereas the remaining WT embryo failed to do so for an unknown reason.
claims.evidence: This is supported by plethysmographic recordings shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The vast majority (9/11) of Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5 never began to generate breathing movements.
claims.source: In direct contrast, the vast majority (9/11) of the Spi1−/− embryos, although they initially expressed a heartbeat, never began to generate breathing movements as evidenced by a virtually flat trace in the plethysmograph recordings (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by plethysmographic recordings shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Two Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5 expressed abnormal breathing behavior for only a few minutes but died rapidly thereafter.
claims.source: The remaining two mutant embryos expressed abnormal breathing behavior for only a few minutes but died rapidly hereafter.
claims.evidence: This is supported by plethysmographic observations.

claims.claim: The anomalies that emerge in the central respiratory networks of Spi1−/− embryos during embryonic development in the absence of microglia are very likely to participate in causing death at birth.
claims.source: Therefore, the anomalies that emerge in the central respiratory networks of Spi1−/− embryos during embryonic development in the absence of microglia are very likely to participate in causing death at birth, with at least one contributing factor being an inability to sustain active breathing movements.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed breathing deficits and neonatal lethality.

claims.claim: An inability to sustain active breathing movements is at least one contributing factor to death at birth in Spi1−/− embryos.
claims.source: Therefore, the anomalies that emerge in the central respiratory networks of Spi1−/− embryos during embryonic development in the absence of microglia are very likely to participate in causing death at birth, with at least one contributing factor being an inability to sustain active breathing movements.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the plethysmographic data showing lack of breathing.

claims.claim: The complete absence of microglia during Spi1−/− mouse embryonic development results in major deficits of the neuronal networks responsible for breathing behavior.
claims.source: Our findings reveal that the complete absence of microglia during Spi1−/− mouse embryonic development results in major deficits of the identified neuronal networks responsible for breathing behavior, specifically in relation to their ability to produce an effective central respiratory command.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Respiratory rhythmogenesis relies on an interaction between distinct neuronal groups located in separate regions of the brainstem.
claims.source: Respiratory rhythmogenesis relies on an interaction between distinct neuronal groups located in separate regions of the brainstem, which normally become sequentially operational during embryogenesis to produce a stable respiratory-related rhythm from 3 days before birth (at E15.5) onwards (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Respiratory networks become sequentially operational during embryogenesis to produce a stable respiratory-related rhythm from E15.5 onwards.
claims.source: Respiratory rhythmogenesis relies on an interaction between distinct neuronal groups located in separate regions of the brainstem, which normally become sequentially operational during embryogenesis to produce a stable respiratory-related rhythm from 3 days before birth (at E15.5) onwards (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: When developing in an environment devoid of microglia, respiratory networks continue to become functional at typical developmental stages, but exhibit anomalies that lead to the generation of an overall slower rhythm.
claims.source: In examining the anatomical and functional characteristics of the two main respiratory neuronal groups (the epF and the preBötC networks) we found that when developing in an environment devoid of microglia, these networks continue to become functional at typical developmental stages, but exhibit anomalies that lead to the generation of an overall slower rhythm and a subsequent inability to sustain breathing behavior at birth.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data from multiple developmental stages.

claims.claim: Respiratory networks developing in an environment devoid of microglia exhibit a subsequent inability to sustain breathing behavior at birth.
claims.source: In examining the anatomical and functional characteristics of the two main respiratory neuronal groups (the epF and the preBötC networks) we found that when developing in an environment devoid of microglia, these networks continue to become functional at typical developmental stages, but exhibit anomalies that lead to the generation of an overall slower rhythm and a subsequent inability to sustain breathing behavior at birth.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the plethysmographic data showing breathing failure.

claims.claim: The deficit in respiratory function is likely to arise from a lack of the normal influence of microglia in regulating cell numbers and the proper wiring of the brainstem circuits responsible for respiratory rhythmogenesis during prenatal development.
claims.source: This deficit is likely to arise from a lack of the normal influence of microglia in regulating cell numbers and the proper wiring of the brainstem circuits responsible for respiratory rhythmogenesis during prenatal development.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed anatomical and functional deficits.

claims.claim: The centrally generated respiratory rhythm results in part from network interactions between the parafacial respiratory group (epF at embryonic stages) and the preBötC.
claims.source: The centrally generated respiratory rhythm results in part from network interactions between the parafacial respiratory group (epF at embryonic stages) and the preBötC (Feldman et al., 2013), both of which are strongly connected to their contralateral counterparts via midline-crossing commissural projections (Wu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The epF and preBötC are both strongly connected to their contralateral counterparts via midline-crossing commissural projections.
claims.source: The centrally generated respiratory rhythm results in part from network interactions between the parafacial respiratory group (epF at embryonic stages) and the preBötC (Feldman et al., 2013), both of which are strongly connected to their contralateral counterparts via midline-crossing commissural projections (Wu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The cycle frequency of respiratory activity is determined by the intrinsic rhythm generated by each half-center network and the strength of the homo- and hetero-network synaptic interactions.
claims.source: Thus, the cycle frequency of respiratory activity is determined by (1) the intrinsic rhythm generated by each half-center network, and (2) the strength of the homo- (preBötC/preBötC; epF/epF) and hetero- (preBötC/epF) network synaptic interactions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge of network interactions.

claims.claim: During embryonic development between E14.5 and E16.5, the epF progressively entrains the intrinsically slower preBötC network, thereby setting the overall respiratory rhythm to an intermediate cycle frequency.
claims.source: During embryonic development these dual controlling processes are established between E14.5 and E16.5 (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009), a period during which the epF (intrinsically active at a higher frequency) progressively entrains the intrinsically slower preBötC network, thereby setting the overall respiratory rhythm to an intermediate cycle frequency (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: At the time of their respective emergence, each respiratory network in the mutant generates rhythmic activity at an abnormally low frequency.
claims.source: Here, we find in the mutant that at the time of their respective emergence, each respiratory network generates rhythmic activity at an abnormally low frequency.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data from both epF and preBötC networks.

claims.claim: The lower frequency of the epF in the mutant is likely to be the consequence of a substantially diminished number of constituent neurons.
claims.source: In the case of the epF, this lower frequency is likely to be the consequence of a substantially diminished number of constituent neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between reduced cell numbers and reduced frequency.

claims.claim: For the preBötC network, anomalies in commissural projections connecting the two bilaterally distributed preBötC neuronal groups are likely to contribute to the slower rhythm generation.
claims.source: For the preBötC network, anomalies in commissural projections connecting the two bilaterally distributed preBötC neuronal groups, resulting in a diminished inter-network synchronization, are likely to contribute to the slower rhythm generation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and functional data for commissural projections.

claims.claim: When the epF and preBötC networks become fully connected at E16.5, their intra- and inter-circuit anomalies result in a reduced frequency of the final respiratory command observed at the level of motor output.
claims.source: Ultimately, when these networks become fully connected at E16.5, their intra- and inter-circuit anomalies result in a reduced frequency of the final respiratory command observed at the level of motor output.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined effects of network deficits on motor output.

claims.claim: Spi1−/− mortality at P0 probably results from multiple functional defaults that are not necessarily exclusively CNS related.
claims.source: While Spi1−/− mortality at P0 probably results from multiple functional defaults that are not necessarily exclusively CNS related (Back et al., 2004), the cause of death is very unlikely related to an immune system deficiency or the development of septicemia that could have arisen due to the absence of microglia.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the known phenotype of the mutant and citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The cause of death in Spi1−/− embryos is very unlikely related to an immune system deficiency or the development of septicemia.
claims.source: While Spi1−/− mortality at P0 probably results from multiple functional defaults that are not necessarily exclusively CNS related (Back et al., 2004), the cause of death is very unlikely related to an immune system deficiency or the development of septicemia that could have arisen due to the absence of microglia.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the timing of death and known biology.

claims.claim: Peripheral causes are likely to be involved in the premature death of animals devoid of microglia.
claims.source: In contrast, peripheral causes are likely to be involved in the premature death of animals devoid of microglia.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the known expression pattern of Spi1.

claims.claim: Spi1 is expressed in hematopoietic stem cells and common lymphoid progenitors impacting not only microglia but also meningeal, choroid plexus, and perivascular macrophages, as well as peripheral immune cells.
claims.source: Indeed, Spi1 is expressed in hematopoietic stem cells and common lymphoid progenitors impacting not only microglia but also meningeal, choroid plexus, and perivascular macrophages, as well as peripheral immune cells (Goldmann et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: No premature death was observed in transgenic mice in which microglia depletion was specifically restricted to the CNS.
claims.source: In a recent study, no premature death was observed in transgenic mice in which microglia depletion was specifically restricted to the CNS (Rojo et al., 2019), thus directly inferring peripheral deficits, possibly including developmental malformations of the upper airways, lungs and heart, as important contributors to neonatal death of Spi1−/− mutants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Peripheral deficits, possibly including developmental malformations of the upper airways, lungs and heart, are important contributors to neonatal death of Spi1−/− mutants.
claims.source: In a recent study, no premature death was observed in transgenic mice in which microglia depletion was specifically restricted to the CNS (Rojo et al., 2019), thus directly inferring peripheral deficits, possibly including developmental malformations of the upper airways, lungs and heart, as important contributors to neonatal death of Spi1−/− mutants.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with CNS-specific microglia depletion models.

claims.claim: Major defaults in overall breathing movement control and/or anomalies in cardiorespiratory activity are very likely contributing significantly to the inability of perinatal Spi1 mutants to survive after birth.
claims.source: Therefore, major defaults in overall breathing movement control (potentially also at the peripheral level) and/or anomalies in cardiorespiratory activity are very likely contributing significantly to the inability of perinatal Spi1 mutants to survive after birth.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observed breathing deficits and known lethality.

claims.claim: Microglia enter and invade the CNS early during development.
claims.source: Microglia are known to enter and invade the CNS early during development (Mosser et al., 2017; Thion and Garel, 2017; Angelim et al., 2018), consistent with an important role in the initial stages of neuronal circuit assembly (Casano and Peri, 2015; Reemst et al., 2016; Mosser et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Microglia play an important role in the initial stages of neuronal circuit assembly.
claims.source: Microglia are known to enter and invade the CNS early during development (Mosser et al., 2017; Thion and Garel, 2017; Angelim et al., 2018), consistent with an important role in the initial stages of neuronal circuit assembly (Casano and Peri, 2015; Reemst et al., 2016; Mosser et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Microglia exhibit a specific spatiotemporal distribution in the embryonic brain, with a characteristic uneven distribution that coincides with the localization of progenitor niches, loci where neurogenesis and cell division occur, near developing blood vessels and the formation of axonal tracts.
claims.source: Moreover, microglia exhibit a specific spatiotemporal distribution in the embryonic brain, with a characteristic uneven distribution that coincides with the localization of progenitor niches, loci where neurogenesis and cell division also occur, near developing blood vessels and the formation of axonal tracts (Ashwell, 1991; Fantin et al., 2010; Verney et al., 2010; Hoshiko et al., 2012; Swinnen et al., 2013; Squarzoni et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: In the developing brainstem, microglia express a preferential spatial distribution, with a higher prevalence in hindbrain motor nuclei and along each side of the hindbrain midline.
claims.source: Similarly, in the developing brainstem, we find that microglia also express a preferential spatial distribution, with a higher prevalence not only in hindbrain motor nuclei but also along each side of the hindbrain midline.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and 3D imaging data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: Most brainstem circuits are bilaterally distributed, with their activities coordinated by commissural axonal projections that cross the midline.
claims.source: This latter observation was of particular interest since most brainstem circuits are bilaterally distributed, with their activities coordinated by commissural axonal projections that cross the midline.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge of brainstem circuit organization.

claims.claim: A strict left/right synchronization of motor output is required to produce a coordinated drive to the left and right diaphragm muscles.
claims.source: This is especially relevant for the central networks organizing the respiratory command, where a strict left/right synchronization of motor output is required to produce a coordinated drive to the left and right diaphragm muscles (Bouvier et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: The commissural connectivity between the central respiratory groups displays redundancy and is extremely complex.
claims.source: The commissural connectivity between the central respiratory groups displays redundancy and is extremely complex.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge of respiratory circuit connectivity.

claims.claim: A bilateral co-activation of the two epF networks occurs as early as E14.5.
claims.source: For example, a bilateral co-activation of the two epF networks occurs as early as E14.5, with synchronizing signals being conveyed through multiple, but still anatomically undefined commissural pathways (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Commissural interneurons between the two preBötC networks participate in the synchronization of bilaterally coordinated contractions of inspiratory effector muscles.
claims.source: In addition, commissural interneurons, both between the two preBötC networks (Smith et al., 1991; Bouvier et al., 2010) and between the ventral respiratory groups (VRGs) that contain pre-motoneurons (Wu et al., 2017), participate in the synchronization of bilaterally coordinated contractions of inspiratory effector muscles.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The anatomical specificity of preBötC commissural connectivity requires the Slit/Robo signaling pathway.
claims.source: At the level of the preBötC, this anatomical specificity requires the Slit/Robo signaling pathway (Bouvier et al., 2010), but might also involve microglia due to the latter's localization near the midline and their known participation in axonal tract formation elsewhere in the CNS (Pont-Lezica et al., 2014; Squarzoni et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Microglia might be involved in preBötC commissural connectivity due to their localization near the midline and their known participation in axonal tract formation elsewhere in the CNS.
claims.source: At the level of the preBötC, this anatomical specificity requires the Slit/Robo signaling pathway (Bouvier et al., 2010), but might also involve microglia due to the latter's localization near the midline and their known participation in axonal tract formation elsewhere in the CNS (Pont-Lezica et al., 2014; Squarzoni et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on microglial localization and known functions, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Inter-preBötC network projections are considerably reduced in the Spi1−/− embryos.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, our findings show firstly, that inter-preBötC network projections are considerably reduced in the Spi1−/− embryos, and second, and correspondingly, in slice preparations isolating the preBötC networks from Spi1−/− embryos at E16.5, the normal functional synchronization between the rhythmogenic half-centers is diminished.
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical labeling data presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: In slice preparations isolating the preBötC networks from Spi1−/− embryos at E16.5, the normal functional synchronization between the rhythmogenic half-centers is diminished.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, our findings show firstly, that inter-preBötC network projections are considerably reduced in the Spi1−/− embryos, and second, and correspondingly, in slice preparations isolating the preBötC networks from Spi1−/− embryos at E16.5, the normal functional synchronization between the rhythmogenic half-centers is diminished.
claims.evidence: This is supported by bilateral electrophysiological recordings presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The redundancy of midline-crossing commissures between other brainstem centers is sufficient to offset the weakened local connections between the preBötC half-centers, thereby enabling the coordination between the downstream left and right motor outputs in the Spi1−/− embryo to be maintained.
claims.source: This apparent compensation is likely attributable to the redundancy of midline-crossing commissures between the other brainstem centers that are sufficient to offset the weakened local connections between the preBötC half-centers (Wu et al., 2017), thereby enabling the coordination between the downstream left and right motor outputs in the Spi1−/− embryo to be maintained.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the maintained bilateral synchrony of phrenic output despite preBötC deficits, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The decreased frequency of phrenic motor output is likely to be the direct consequence of the slower rhythmic command signal emanating from the interacting epF and preBötC networks.
claims.source: On the one hand, the decreased frequency is likely to be the direct consequence of the slower rhythmic command signal emanating from the interacting epF and preBötC networks, both groups separately generating a respiratory-related rhythmic activity at an abnormally slow frequency.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed slow frequencies at multiple levels of the respiratory network.

claims.claim: The increase in motor burst duration could have arisen from a reduction in the coordination within the preBötC networks and between inspiratory interneurons and VRG pre-motoneurons.
claims.source: On the other hand, the increase in motor burst duration could have arisen from a reduction in the coordination within the preBötC networks and between inspiratory interneurons and VRG pre-motoneurons.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observed coordination deficits.

claims.claim: Reduced coordination within the preBötC networks would lead to a less synchronized drive to target motoneurons and thus an overall increase in phrenic motor burst duration in each cycle.
claims.source: This in turn would lead to a less synchronized drive to target motoneurons and thus an overall increase in phrenic motor burst duration in each cycle.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying increased burst duration.

claims.claim: The phrenic motor nucleus itself might be affected in the mutant, especially in light of the finding that microglia are normally present in high density in the different brainstem motor nuclei.
claims.source: Another possibility is that the phrenic motor nucleus itself is affected in the mutant, especially in light of our finding that microglia are normally present in high density in the different brainstem motor nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observed microglial distribution in motor nuclei.

claims.claim: When developing in the absence of microglia, the firing properties of motoneuronal groups, including those in the phrenic nucleus, might be directly affected, thereby contributing to the observed increase in phrenic burst duration.
claims.source: Thus, when developing in the absence of microglia, the firing properties of these motoneuronal groups, including those in the phrenic nucleus, might be directly affected, thereby contributing to the observed increase in phrenic burst duration.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying the observed phenotype.

claims.claim: The essential regulation of neuronal numbers in the construction of neural circuitry during development occurs through several mechanisms in which microglia may participate: neuronal death, survival, and migration.
claims.source: The essential regulation of neuronal numbers in the construction of neural circuitry during development occurs through several mechanisms in which microglia may participate: neuronal death, survival, and migration (Thion and Garel, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: In the mouse respiratory system, epF neurons originate in the dB2 domain of rhombomere 5 (r5) then migrate conjointly with facial motoneurons to reach their final location in r6 by E14.5.
claims.source: In the mouse respiratory system, epF neurons originate in the dB2 domain of rhombomere 5 (r5) then migrate conjointly with facial motoneurons to reach their final location in r6 by E14.5, near the ventral surface of the hindbrain and below the facial motor nucleus (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011; Mellen and Thoby-Brisson, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Perturbations in epF formation have been detected in different mouse lines genetically modified for transcription factors known to specify epF neuronal components, such as Phox2b, Egr2, Lbx1, and Atoh1.
claims.source: Perturbations in epF formation have been detected in different mouse lines genetically modified for transcription factors known to specify epF neuronal components, such as Phox2b, Egr2, Lbx1, and Atoh1 (Pagliardini et al., 2008; Dubreuil et al., 2009; Rose et al., 2009; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009; Ruffault et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: In most transcription factor mutant mouse lines, the number of epF neurons was found to be drastically reduced, with significant resultant effects on epF network function, including both rhythmogenesis and loss of CO2/pH responsiveness.
claims.source: In most cases, the number of epF neurons was found to be drastically reduced in these mutant animal, with significant resultant effects on epF network function, including both rhythmogenesis and loss of CO2/pH responsiveness.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: In the Spi1−/−, the reduction of neurons constituting the epF group presumably results from an abnormally high level of epF cell death and/or migratory dysfunction.
claims.source: In the Spi1−/−, the reduction (by ~31%) of neurons constituting the epF group presumably results from an abnormally high level of epF cell death and/or migratory dysfunction.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the reduced epF cell number.

claims.claim: The diminished epF population size in Spi1−/− embryos probably explains the production of a slower epF rhythm at E14.5.
claims.source: This diminished epF population size in turn probably explains the production of a slower (by 33%) epF rhythm at E14.5, and indeed, also that of fictive respiration observed from E16.5 onwards in isolated hindbrain preparations, where rhythmic burst activity in the phrenic motor roots arises from both the epF and the now active preBötC generators operating in combination.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between reduced cell numbers and reduced frequency.

claims.claim: At E16.5, the epF is known to entrain the preBötC.
claims.source: Since at this later embryonic stage the epF is known to entrain the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009), a slower intrinsic rhythm generated by the epF in the mutant will drive the preBötC at an equally reduced frequency (but note, the preBötC itself generates a slower rhythm; see below), with a resultant production of slower phrenic motor bursting.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: A slower intrinsic rhythm generated by the epF in the mutant will drive the preBötC at an equally reduced frequency, with a resultant production of slower phrenic motor bursting.
claims.source: Since at this later embryonic stage the epF is known to entrain the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009), a slower intrinsic rhythm generated by the epF in the mutant will drive the preBötC at an equally reduced frequency (but note, the preBötC itself generates a slower rhythm; see below), with a resultant production of slower phrenic motor bursting.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known entrainment relationship and observed frequencies.

claims.claim: The epF's intrinsic sensitivity to pH changes at E14.5 is preserved in the mutant.
claims.source: In contrast, the epF's intrinsic sensitivity to pH changes at E14.5 is preserved in the mutant, indicating that despite a reduction in constituent neurons, the normal chemosensing capability of this neuronal group is preserved.
claims.evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing pH responsiveness in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Despite a reduction in constituent neurons, the normal chemosensing capability of the epF neuronal group is preserved in Spi1−/− embryos.
claims.source: In contrast, the epF's intrinsic sensitivity to pH changes at E14.5 is preserved in the mutant, indicating that despite a reduction in constituent neurons, the normal chemosensing capability of this neuronal group is preserved.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the preserved pH responsiveness.

claims.claim: The epF's chemosensitivity property persists later in development, since acidifying the aCSF bathing isolated brainstem preparations at E18.5 still evoked a frequency increase of respiratory activity recorded at the level of phrenic roots.
claims.source: This functional property also persists later in development, since acidifying the aCSF bathing isolated brainstem preparations at E18.5 still evoked a frequency increase of respiratory activity recorded at the level of phrenic roots.
claims.evidence: This is supported by phrenic nerve recordings under different pH conditions shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Although the complete neuronal composition of epF circuitry early during embryonic development depends on the presence of microglia, in the latter's absence the network's basic rhythmogenic and chemosensitivity properties remain.
claims.source: Together these findings therefore indicate that although the complete neuronal composition of epF circuitry early during embryonic development depends on the presence of microglia, nevertheless, in the latter's absence the network's basic rhythmogenic and chemosensitivity properties remain.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined anatomical and functional data for the epF network.

claims.claim: The preBötC network originates from the V0v domain in r6/7.
claims.source: The preBötC network originates from the V0v domain in r6/7, and is composed of a heterogeneous population of Dbx1-specified interneurons that migrate radially from their territory of origin (near the sulcus limitans bordering the fourth ventricle) to their final position in the ventro-lateral area in the vicinity of the nucleus ambiguus (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Mellen and Thoby-Brisson, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The preBötC network is composed of a heterogeneous population of Dbx1-specified interneurons that migrate radially from their territory of origin to their final position in the ventro-lateral area in the vicinity of the nucleus ambiguus.
claims.source: The preBötC network originates from the V0v domain in r6/7, and is composed of a heterogeneous population of Dbx1-specified interneurons that migrate radially from their territory of origin (near the sulcus limitans bordering the fourth ventricle) to their final position in the ventro-lateral area in the vicinity of the nucleus ambiguus (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Mellen and Thoby-Brisson, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The preBötC network in the mutant is sufficiently preserved in its ability to produce inspiration-related rhythmic activity, albeit at a slower frequency.
claims.source: However, our physiological results indicate that this network in the mutant is sufficiently preserved, if affected at all, in its ability to produce inspiration-related rhythmic activity, albeit at a slower frequency.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological recordings showing rhythmic activity.

claims.claim: The frequency reduction in the preBötC could result from a diminished connectivity between inspiratory interneurons as indicated by the reduced number of commissural projections between the preBötC half-centers.
claims.source: This frequency reduction could result from a diminished connectivity between inspiratory interneurons as indicated by the reduced number of commissural projections between the preBötC half-centers (as discussed above) and a consequent less efficient synchronization between the two preBötC groups.

results.result: Microglia are present in the embryonic brainstem with a preferential distribution in motor nuclei (facial and hypoglossal) and along the midline from E14.5 to E18.5.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C30 are supported by immunostaining (Figure 1) and 3D imaging with density mapping (Figure 2) showing consistent microglial localization patterns across developmental stages. The data converge to demonstrate a non-uniform distribution with enrichment in specific anatomical regions.

results.result: The Spi1−/− mutant mouse completely lacks microglia in the nervous system.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C28 are supported by citation to prior literature (Back et al., 2004) and confirmed by complete absence of Iba1 immunostaining in mutant brainstem tissue at all rostro-caudal levels examined (Figure 1P-T).

results.result: At E14.5, the epF network in Spi1−/− embryos shows a 31% reduction in neuron number, reduced facial nucleus extension, and generates rhythmic activity at a significantly slower frequency (8.2 vs 12.4 calcium transients/min), while maintaining chemosensitivity to pH changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C38 are well-supported by converging anatomical (immunostaining cell counts, Figure 3A-D) and functional (calcium imaging, Figure 3E-F) data. The preservation of pH responsiveness despite anatomical and frequency deficits is clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical testing (p<0.01).

results.result: At E16.5, the preBötC network in Spi1−/− embryos generates spontaneous rhythmic activity at a reduced frequency (5.5 vs 7.6 bursts/min) with longer burst durations (1.23 vs 1.00 s), but maintains rhythm regularity and responsiveness to Substance P.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by electrophysiological recordings from transverse brainstem slices (Figure 4). Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.001) for frequency and duration changes, while regularity (coefficient of variation) and SP responsiveness are preserved, indicating functional network integrity despite deficits.

results.result: Spi1−/− embryos show considerably reduced commissural projections between bilateral preBötC networks and significantly wider delays between bilateral bursts (48.9 vs -4 ms), indicating weakened synchronization that likely contributes to altered respiratory rhythm generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by anatomical labeling of commissural fibers (Figure 5A) and bilateral electrophysiological recordings (Figure 5B) showing significant desynchronization (p<0.05). The causal link between anatomical and functional deficits is a reasonable inference given the known role of commissural connections.

results.result: At E18.5, phrenic motor output in Spi1−/− embryos shows reduced frequency (10.6 vs 14 bursts/min) and longer burst durations (948 vs 843 ms), but maintains chemosensitivity to pH changes with significant frequency increases upon acidification in both genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 are supported by phrenic nerve recordings from isolated brainstem preparations (Figure 6A-C). Statistical significance is demonstrated for frequency and duration differences (p<0.001), and pH responsiveness is preserved in both genotypes, confirming functional chemosensitivity despite other deficits.

results.result: Bilateral synchronization of phrenic motor output is maintained in Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5, with similar delays between left and right C4 bursts compared to WT (0.8 vs 2.07 ms, p=0.6).
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 are supported by bilateral phrenic nerve recordings (Figure 6D) showing no significant difference in synchronization between genotypes. This finding is somewhat unexpected given the preBötC commissural deficits, but the authors reasonably attribute this to redundancy in other commissural pathways.

results.result: At E18.5, 9/11 Spi1−/− embryos fail to generate breathing movements ex utero compared to 14/15 WT embryos that breathe normally, indicating that respiratory network abnormalities contribute to neonatal lethality.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 are supported by plethysmographic recordings (Figure 7) showing clear differences in breathing behavior. The inference that respiratory deficits contribute to lethality is reasonable given the dramatic phenotype, though the authors appropriately acknowledge that other factors may also contribute.

results.result: The complete absence of microglia during embryonic development results in major deficits in respiratory network function, including slower rhythm generation and inability to sustain breathing at birth, likely arising from defects in cell number regulation and circuit wiring.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C67-C69, C14, and C142 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by converging anatomical and functional data across multiple developmental stages and levels of the respiratory network. The mechanistic interpretation is reasonable given the observed deficits, though direct causal links require further investigation.

results.result: Both respiratory networks (epF and preBötC) generate abnormally slow rhythms in the mutant at their respective emergence times, with the epF deficit likely due to reduced neuron numbers and the preBötC deficit likely due to impaired commissural connectivity, ultimately resulting in reduced frequency of the final respiratory motor command.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 synthesize findings from multiple experiments and represent reasonable mechanistic inferences based on the correlation between anatomical deficits and functional consequences. The logic connecting network-level deficits to motor output is sound and supported by the data.

results.result: Inter-preBötC commissural projections are reduced in Spi1−/− embryos with diminished functional synchronization between half-centers, but redundant commissures from other brainstem centers compensate to maintain bilateral coordination of downstream motor outputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are supported by anatomical data (Figure 5A) and bilateral recordings at different levels (preBötC vs phrenic). The compensation hypothesis is a reasonable inference to explain the apparent discrepancy between preBötC desynchronization and maintained phrenic synchrony, supported by citation to prior work on commissural redundancy.

results.result: Neonatal death in Spi1−/− mutants likely results from multiple factors including both central respiratory deficits and peripheral abnormalities, as Spi1 affects multiple cell types beyond microglia and CNS-specific microglia depletion does not cause premature death.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 are supported by citation to prior literature (Back et al., 2004; Goldmann et al., 2016; Rojo et al., 2019) and represent reasonable speculation about the multifactorial nature of the lethal phenotype. The comparison with CNS-specific depletion models strengthens the argument for peripheral contributions.

results.result: The increased phrenic burst duration in Spi1−/− embryos could result from reduced coordination within preBötC networks and between inspiratory interneurons and pre-motoneurons, or from direct effects on phrenic motoneurons themselves.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 represent mechanistic speculation about the causes of increased burst duration. While the hypotheses are plausible given the observed deficits and microglial distribution, they lack direct experimental support. Additional experiments targeting specific circuit components would be needed to distinguish between these possibilities.

results.result: The reduced epF neuron number in Spi1−/− embryos (31% reduction) presumably results from abnormal cell death and/or migration, explaining the slower epF rhythm, though basic rhythmogenic and chemosensitive properties are preserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109, C111, and C115 are supported by the anatomical and functional data for the epF network. The mechanistic speculation about cell death/migration is reasonable given known microglial functions, though direct evidence is lacking. The preservation of basic network properties despite reduced cell numbers is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: The preBötC network in Spi1−/− embryos maintains the ability to generate rhythmic activity despite slower frequency, potentially due to reduced commissural connectivity, altered synaptic properties, or loss of microglial BDNF signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119, C123, and C128 combine demonstrated findings (preserved rhythmogenesis) with mechanistic speculation. While the hypotheses are plausible and grounded in known microglial functions (synaptic regulation, BDNF release), they lack direct experimental support in this study. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities requiring further investigation.

results.result: Microglia show preferential localization along the hindbrain midline where commissural projections cross, suggesting potential involvement in commissural connectivity development, consistent with their known role in axonal tract formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C88 and C95 are supported by immunostaining and 3D imaging data (Figures 1-2) showing midline enrichment, combined with the observed commissural deficits in the mutant (Figure 5). The speculation about microglial involvement in commissural development is reasonable given the spatial correlation and known functions, though direct mechanistic evidence is lacking.

results.result: Despite anatomical and functional disturbances, the absence of microglia does not completely prevent formation of circuits capable of respiratory rhythmogenesis, likely due to redundant developmental mechanisms for this vital function.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 are supported by the observation that rhythmic activity persists across all developmental stages in the mutant, albeit with deficits. The inference about redundant mechanisms is reasonable speculation to explain the partial preservation of function, though the specific mechanisms remain undefined.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about microglial functions and respiratory network development are established in the literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C15-C22 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These provide the necessary context and motivation for the current study.

results.result: The timing of respiratory network emergence (epF at E14.5, preBötC at E16.5) is established in prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 are supported by citations to prior literature and are consistent with the experimental design of the current study. However, there is a minor discrepancy: the abstract states preBötC emerges at E16.5, while the introduction cites E15.5 (C20). This inconsistency should be noted but does not affect the main results.

results.result: Prior work on microglial roles in CNS development and respiratory control provides context for the current study, which represents the first description of microglial distribution and function in the embryonic hindbrain respiratory networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87, C135-C141 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature and accurately position the novelty of the current work. The claim of being the first description of microglial distribution in embryonic hindbrain respiratory networks appears justified.

results.result: Established knowledge about respiratory network organization, development, connectivity, and neuromodulation provides the framework for interpreting the observed deficits in Spi1−/− embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66, C70-C73, C89-C94, C104-C107, C110, C116-C117, C120-C122, C124-C127, C132-C134 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide essential context for understanding the significance of the experimental findings.
